recipes.title: Classic Chicken Broth
recipes.about: Chicken broth is the oldest and most restorative dish in the canon. It has been made in British kitchens for centuries, prescribed by doctors and offered by mothers alike as the first response to illness, cold, and frailty. It is the most elemental thing a carer can make: warm, deeply nourishing, gentle on the stomach, and profoundly comforting. For clients who can manage little else, a cup of good broth is never nothing.

ingredients.item: Free-range chicken carcass or 2 chicken thighs on the bone
Brown onion, halved (skin on for colour)

method: Place the chicken carcass or thighs in a large saucepan. Cover with the cold water. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer over a medium heat. As the liquid heats, grey foam will rise to the surface: skim this away carefully with a ladle or large spoon. This takes patience but makes a cleaner, clearer broth.
Once the foam has subsided, add the onion, carrot, celery, leek, parsley stalks, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Do not add salt yet.

Reduce the heat to the lowest possible simmer. The surface should tremble gently, not bubble vigorously. A hard boil makes a cloudy, bitter broth. Simmer uncovered for at least 1 hour 30 minutes, and up to 2 hours for a deeper flavour.

Strain the broth through a fine sieve into a clean saucepan, pressing gently on the vegetables to extract all the liquid. Discard the solids. If using chicken thighs, pick the meat from the bones and set aside: it can be returned to the broth or used separately.
Taste and season with salt. The broth should taste clean, golden, and deeply savoury. If it tastes thin, return to the heat and simmer uncovered for a further 20 minutes to concentrate.
Serve warm in a cup or bowl, with or without the shredded chicken meat. A few drops of good olive oil on the surface add richness and calories.
key_nutrients: Collagen and gelatine from the bones: supports joint health and gut lining integrity.
Easily absorbed minerals including calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus extracted during the long simmer.
High fluid content: one of the most effective ways to support hydration in clients who do not drink enough.
Glycine from the connective tissue: supports sleep quality and muscle repair.
Light on the digestive system: ideal for clients who are unwell, post-operative, or have very little appetite.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: the smell of broth simmering is one of the most evocative of all cooking aromas. For many clients it will trigger strong, positive memories of childhood kitchens.
Dysphagia: at IDDSI Level 1 (thin liquid) this is suitable for most clients with swallowing difficulties. For thickened fluid requirements, thicken to the prescribed level.
COPD: warm, easily taken fluids reduce the effort of eating. Small, frequent cups of broth throughout the day support both hydration and calorie intake.
Appetite: broth is one of the few things most clients will accept even when they feel too unwell or too low in appetite to eat anything else.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Strain thoroughly to ensure no particles remain. Suitable as a thin fluid for most dysphagia profiles.
Add a measured amount of prescribed thickening agent to achieve the required consistency. Always measure precisely and stir thoroughly.
Blend any returned chicken meat to a completely smooth paste and whisk into the broth. The result should be a smooth, slightly enriched broth. Pass through a fine sieve.
Return the picked chicken meat to the broth and serve as a simple, clear soup. Add soft-cooked noodles or pearl barley for a more substantial dish.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Chicken broth is one of the most universally comforting foods in British life. Many clients will associate it strongly with being cared for during childhood illness. Simply saying "I've made you some broth" carries a weight of reassurance that few other dishes can match. Offer it in a cup if a bowl feels too much.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a warmed cup or small soup bowl. A few shreds of chicken meat and a single sprig of flat-leaf parsley make it look considered without fuss. For clients with very small appetites, offer a small cup first rather than a full bowl.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Broth is naturally low in sodium if made from scratch, but do watch for seasoning: clients with hypertension or heart failure should have very lightly salted broth. Ensure the broth is strained to a thin, clear liquid for dysphagia clients: any particles or fibres are a safety risk at IDDSI Level 1.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Make a large batch at the weekend and freeze in individual cup-sized portions. A good broth keeps in the fridge for 3 days and in the freezer for 3 months. Reheat gently in a small saucepan: do not boil, as this diminishes the flavour.

recipes.title: Leek and Potato Soup
recipes.about: Leek and potato soup is a cornerstone of British home cooking, simple in its ingredients and deeply satisfying in the bowl. It became a staple of the British kitchen in the mid-twentieth century and for many clients of a certain age it is the default soup, the one they think of first when the weather turns cold. Made properly, with good stock and a generous hand with the leeks, it is silky, sweet, and warming.

ingredients.item: Leeks, white and pale green parts only, washed and sliced
Maris Piper potatoes, peeled and roughly diced
Chives or flat-leaf parsley to serve

method: Melt the butter in a large, heavy-based saucepan over a low heat. Add the onion and leeks with a pinch of salt. Cook very gently for 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until completely soft and sweet but not coloured. Do not rush this step: the sweetness of the leeks is the foundation of the soup.
Add the garlic and cook for a further minute. Add the diced potatoes and stir to coat in the buttery leeks.
Pour in the stock, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook for 20-25 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender when pierced with a knife.
Remove from the heat. Using a stick blender, blend the soup until completely smooth. Alternatively, ladle into a jug blender in batches, being careful with the hot liquid.
Return to the heat, stir in the cream if using, and heat through gently. Taste and season carefully with salt and white pepper.
Serve in a warmed bowl, finished with a swirl of cream and a few snipped chives.
key_nutrients: Potassium from the leeks and potatoes: supports heart health and blood pressure regulation.
Folate from the leeks: important for cell repair and reducing homocysteine levels.
Vitamin C from both leeks and potatoes: supports immune function and iron absorption.
Fibre: supports digestive health and constipation prevention.
Calories from the butter and cream: an excellent vehicle for calorie enrichment.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: naturally low in saturated fat before the cream is added. Use a light touch with the cream and omit salt for clients with hypertension.
Diabetes: the potato content raises blood sugar modestly. Reduce the potato and increase the leek ratio for clients who need tighter glucose control.
Appetite: smooth and easy to eat, this soup is often accepted when solid food is not. Enrich generously with cream for clients at risk of malnutrition.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Blend until completely smooth and pass through a fine sieve for the cleanest result. The soup should fall slowly from a spoon and hold its shape briefly.
Blend less thoroughly, leaving very small soft pieces of leek. Check no pieces exceed 4mm.
Serve as made, smooth and creamy. Offer a small piece of soft bread alongside if appropriate.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: For most clients over 70, leek and potato soup is among the most familiar of all dishes. It is associated strongly with autumn and winter, with mothers and grandmothers, and with the sense of being fed and looked after. Ask the client whether they prefer it smooth or with a little texture: the conversation itself is a pleasant one.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: A smooth, cream-coloured soup needs a considered finish. A thin swirl of cream, a few drops of green chive oil (blended chives with olive oil), or a scattering of snipped chives all add visual distinction without complexity. Serve in a warmed bowl.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Leeks are high in potassium: this soup should be avoided or modified for clients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Omit the leek green tops entirely and reduce the potato portion for the most restricted CKD diets. Always check the care plan.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This soup keeps well in the fridge for 2-3 days and freezes for up to 3 months. Make a larger batch and freeze in individual portions. To reheat, warm gently in a saucepan with a splash of stock or milk to restore the smooth consistency.

recipes.title: Roasted Tomato and Basil Soup
condition_tags: ! High in potassium from the tomatoes: use with caution for clients with CKD. Reduce
portion size or substitute with roasted red pepper for a lower-potassium version.
recipes.about: Roasting transforms tinned or fresh tomatoes, concentrating their natural sugars and producing a soup of a deeper, richer colour and flavour than the stovetop method alone achieves. This is a soup with a very British modern history: it became a household staple from the 1990s onwards and will be familiar to almost all clients. It is brighter and more vivid than many soups in this chapter, and works well as a starter for clients who need their appetite stimulated before a main course.

ingredients.item: Ripe plum tomatoes, or 2 x 400g tins of good plum tomatoes

method: Preheat the oven to 200°C / 180°C fan / Gas 6.

If using fresh tomatoes, halve them and place cut-side up on a large roasting tray. If using tinned tomatoes, pour them onto the tray and spread out. Add the onion quarters and unpeeled garlic cloves. Drizzle generously with olive oil and season with salt and pepper.
Roast in the preheated oven for 35-40 minutes until the tomatoes are caramelised at the edges and the onion is soft and golden. The garlic should be soft inside its skin.
Allow to cool slightly, then squeeze the roasted garlic from its skins directly into a large saucepan. Add all the roasted tomatoes and onion, scraping up any caramelised juices from the tray.
Pour in the stock and add the sugar and most of the basil. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes.
Blend until completely smooth using a stick blender. Pass through a fine sieve, pressing firmly, to remove skin and seeds. Return to the pan.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Add a little more sugar if the tomatoes are acidic. Stir in the cream if using. Serve hot, finished with the remaining basil leaves torn over the top.
key_nutrients: Lycopene from the roasted tomatoes: a powerful antioxidant associated with reduced cancer risk, and better absorbed from cooked tomatoes than raw.
Vitamin C: supports immune function and iron absorption.
Vitamin K: important for bone health.
Potassium: supports heart health and blood pressure, though note the caution for CKD clients.
Olive oil provides heart-healthy monounsaturated fats and additional calories.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: tomatoes and olive oil are both associated with cardiovascular benefit. Use without cream and with minimal salt for clients with hypertension.
Cancer support: lycopene from roasted tomatoes is one of the most studied anti-cancer nutrients. This soup is an easy and delicious way to include it regularly.
Appetite: the bright colour and vivid flavour of this soup can stimulate appetite in clients who are disinterested in food. Serve as a small starter portion if appetite is poor.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Blend thoroughly and pass through a fine sieve to remove all skin and seeds. The result should be completely smooth. Check consistency: it should fall slowly from a spoon.
nd less thoroughly, leaving very small soft pieces. Sieve to ove any skin. Check no pieces exceed 4mm.
ve smooth with a swirl of cream and fresh basil. Offer a small ce of soft bread or a cheese straw alongside.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Tomato soup has an almost universal nostalgic resonance in Britain, partly through the tinned variety which was a staple of family lunches from the 1950s onwards. This homemade version is considerably superior and the comparison is often a pleasant conversation starter. Many clients will comment that it is "so much better than the tin" and that in itself is a small pleasure.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The deep red-orange colour of this soup is its greatest visual asset. Serve in a white bowl to contrast. A thin swirl of cream, a single basil leaf, and a few drops of good olive oil are all that is needed. For clients who enjoy a little texture, a small crouton or a cheese straw alongside adds interest.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Tomatoes are moderately high in potassium: avoid for clients with CKD or modify with a smaller portion. Tinned tomatoes vary considerably in acidity and sweetness: taste before serving and adjust the sugar accordingly. The soup should not be sharp or acidic when served.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This soup can be made entirely from tinned tomatoes, which are actually superior to out-of-season fresh tomatoes and require no preparation. Make a large batch and freeze in individual portions. The roasting step can be done in advance and the roasted tomatoes stored in the fridge for up to 2 days before making the soup.

recipes.title: Mulligatawny Soup
recipes.about: Mulligatawny is one of the great dishes of the British colonial kitchen, brought back from India and adapted by Victorian cooks into something entirely its own: spiced, rich, and deeply savoury. It appeared on the menus of London clubs and country house dining rooms throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and will be strongly remembered by clients who grew up in households where it was a regular feature. It is warming without being fiery, aromatic without being overpowering, and more interesting than most soups in a care setting.

ingredients.item: Chicken thighs, skinless and boneless, diced

method: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based saucepan over a medium heat. Add the onion and carrot with a pinch of salt. Cook for 8-10 minutes until softened and beginning to colour.
Add the garlic and ginger and cook for a further 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant.

Add the curry powder, cumin, coriander, and turmeric. Stir well and cook the spices for 1-2 minutes until fragrant. This step is important: cooking the spices in the fat rather than adding them with the liquid makes a significant difference to the final depth of flavour.
Add the diced chicken and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 3-4 minutes until sealed on all sides.
Add the tinned tomatoes and stir well. Add the lentils and pour in the stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 25-30 minutes until the lentils are completely soft and the chicken is cooked through.
Remove from the heat. For a smooth soup, blend thoroughly with a stick blender. For a more textured finish, blend only half the soup and stir together. Stir in the coconut milk or cream.
Return to the heat, taste, and season. The soup should be warmly spiced, rich, and golden. Serve with a little fresh coriander if the client enjoys it.
key_nutrients: Protein from the chicken and lentils: excellent for muscle maintenance and wound healing.
Fibre from the lentils: supports digestive health and constipation prevention.
Curcumin from the turmeric: a powerful anti-inflammatory compound of particular interest for joint and neurological health.
Iron from the lentils: supports energy and immune function.
Coconut milk or cream adds important calories for clients at risk of malnutrition.
good_for_conditions: Appetite: the aromatic spicing of mulligatawny stimulates appetite effectively. The familiar-but-interesting flavour profile often works well for clients who have grown bored of plainer soups.
Dementia: many clients aged 75 and over will have a strong association with this dish from childhood or early adult life. The aroma of the spices is distinctive and memory-triggering.
Heart health: lentils, turmeric, and lean chicken are all associated with cardiovascular benefit. Use coconut milk sparingly for clients with elevated cholesterol.

iddsi_table.adaptation: lend until completely smooth and pass through a fine sieve. The piced lentil base blends very smoothly. Check no fibrous pieces of hicken remain.
lend thoroughly but not completely, leaving very small moist ieces of chicken and soft lentil. Check all pieces are under 4mm.
erve with texture: shreds of tender chicken, soft lentils, and a wirl of cream. Offer a small piece of soft naan or white bread longside if appropriate.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Mulligatawny was a feature of British dining room life from the Victorian era through to the mid-twentieth century and many clients will have a strong association with it from childhood or from dining in clubs and hotels. It is worth mentioning the name before serving: the word itself often triggers a positive response. Ask whether the client has had it before and how.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The golden-amber colour of this soup is striking. Serve in a warmed white bowl with a swirl of cream or coconut milk and a single small leaf of coriander. For clients who dislike coriander, omit entirely: a few drops of olive oil work equally well as a finish.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Keep the spicing mild: this is not a hot curry. Use a mild curry powder only and taste before serving. For clients who are sensitive to spice, reduce the curry powder to 1 teaspoon. Lentils are moderately high in potassium: reduce the quantity for clients with CKD.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The lentils thicken this soup naturally as it cools and reheats. Add an extra splash of stock when reheating to restore the correct consistency. The soup freezes very well and the flavour improves after a day in the fridge.

recipes.title: Butternut Squash and Ginger Soup
recipes.about: Butternut squash soup is a relative newcomer to the British table, becoming popular from the 1990s onwards, but it has quickly established itself as a modern classic. Its vivid orange colour, natural sweetness, and velvety texture make it one of the most visually appealing and easy-to-eat soups in this book. The ginger adds warmth and digestive benefit without sharpness. It is a particularly good choice for clients who need their appetite stimulated or who have been unwell.

ingredients.item: Butternut squash, peeled, deseeded, and diced into 3cm cubes
Fresh ginger, peeled and roughly sliced
Double cream or coconut milk to serve

method: Preheat the oven to 200°C / 180°C fan / Gas 6.

Place the squash cubes and onion on a large roasting tray. Tuck in the unpeeled garlic cloves and the ginger slices. Drizzle generously with olive oil and season with salt, pepper, and the cumin if using. Toss to coat.
Roast for 30-35 minutes until the squash is golden at the edges, completely tender, and caramelised. The roasting is what gives this soup its depth of flavour: do not rush it.
Squeeze the garlic from its skins into a large saucepan. Add all the roasted squash, onion, and ginger. Pour in the stock.
Blend until completely smooth using a stick blender. The soup should be thick and velvety.
Return to the heat. If the soup is very thick, add a little more stock to achieve a good pouring consistency. Taste and season.
Serve in a warmed bowl, finished with a swirl of cream or coconut milk and a small grinding of black pepper.
key_nutrients: Beta-carotene from the squash: a powerful antioxidant converted to vitamin A in the body. Important for immune function, vision, and skin health.
Gingerols from the fresh ginger: anti-inflammatory compounds that support digestive health and reduce nausea.
Vitamin C: supports immune function and collagen synthesis.
Potassium: supports heart health. Note the caution for CKD clients.
Fibre: the squash provides good dietary fibre to support digestive regularity.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: the vivid orange colour of this soup is visually engaging and easy to identify. Strong visual contrast between food and bowl supports independence at mealtimes for clients with dementia.
Diabetes: butternut squash has a moderate glycaemic index and is much lower in starch than potato-based soups. A good choice for clients managing blood sugar, served without bread.
Cancer support: beta-carotene and vitamin C are both important antioxidants. The anti-inflammatory properties of ginger are of particular interest in cancer care.

iddsi_table.adaptation: The roasted squash blends to an almost perfectly smooth consistency. Pass through a sieve for the cleanest result. Adjust consistency with extra warm stock.
Blend less thoroughly, leaving very small soft pieces. Check no pieces exceed 4mm. Add extra stock to ensure the mixture is sufficiently moist.
Serve smooth with a swirl of cream. A few toasted pumpkin seeds on top add texture and visual interest for clients who can manage them safely.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Butternut squash soup is more recent than many dishes in this book, but it has become widely familiar and is often associated with the pleasure of autumn. Many clients will have encountered it in good restaurants or made it themselves in their earlier years. The beautiful colour alone tends to provoke a positive response.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The deep amber-orange of this soup is its greatest asset. Serve in a white bowl, finish with a spiral of cream or coconut milk, and perhaps a few drops of chilli oil for clients who enjoy a little heat. The colour contrast is inherently appetising.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Butternut squash is moderately high in potassium: modify or avoid for clients with CKD. The ginger is gentle but can occasionally cause heartburn in clients with gastric reflux: reduce or omit if this is a concern.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This soup improves overnight as the flavours deepen. Make a large batch on the weekend, freeze in portions, and reheat as needed. The roasting step can be done in advance and the squash kept in the fridge for up to 2 days before making the soup.

recipes.title: Bone Broth
recipes.about: Bone broth is distinct from a simple chicken broth in both method and character. The long cooking time and the roasting of the bones before simmering produce a much darker, richer liquid with a depth of mineral content and collagen that a shorter broth cannot match. It has been made in British kitchens for centuries and is experiencing a well-founded revival in nutritional circles. For clients with bone density concerns, Parkinson's, or low appetite, it is one of the most nourishing things you can offer.

ingredients.item: Chicken, beef, or lamb bones (ask a butcher)
Apple cider vinegar (helps extract minerals from the bones)

method: Preheat the oven to 220°C / 200°C fan / Gas 7.

Spread the bones on a large roasting tray and roast in the preheated oven for 30-35 minutes until deeply golden and caramelised. This step is essential: it is what gives bone broth its dark colour and rich flavour. Do not skip it.

Transfer the roasted bones to a large stockpot or slow cooker. Pour in the cold water and add the apple cider vinegar. Allow to stand for 30 minutes before heating: this acidic soak helps draw minerals from the bones.
Add the onion, carrot, celery, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns, and herbs. Bring very slowly to the gentlest possible simmer.

Skim off any foam that rises in the first 20-30 minutes. Then leave to simmer, barely trembling, for a minimum of 4 hours and up to 6 hours. The longer it simmers, the richer and more gelatinous the result. A slow cooker on low overnight is ideal.
Strain through a fine sieve into a clean saucepan or heatproof container. Discard the solids. Season with salt only at the end.
Cool completely. When refrigerated, a good bone broth will set to a jelly: this is a sign of its high gelatine content and is exactly what you want. Skim the fat from the surface before reheating.
key_nutrients: Collagen and gelatine: supports joint cartilage, gut lining integrity, and skin health. The long cooking time extracts far more than a short broth.
Calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus: extracted directly from the bones during the long acid simmer. Significant contribution to bone mineral density.
Glycine and proline: amino acids that support sleep quality, muscle repair, and gut health.
Glutamine: supports intestinal lining integrity, particularly important for clients on long-term medication.
Almost zero carbohydrate: suitable for diabetic clients without any blood sugar impact.
good_for_conditions: Bone health: one of the most direct dietary sources of bone minerals. Particularly valuable for clients with osteoporosis or osteopenia.
Parkinson's: warm, easy-to-take liquids that require no chewing. The glycine content may support sleep quality. Can be sipped from a cup or taken through a straw.
Appetite: highly nourishing with very little volume. A small cup of enriched bone broth provides significant nutritional benefit even for clients who manage very little food.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as strained, at a gentle warmth. Suitable for thin fluid IDDSI profiles. Thicken with a prescribed agent if required.
Add a measured amount of prescribed thickening agent. Stir well and check consistency before serving.
Serve in a warmed cup or small bowl. A few soft-cooked noodles, soft vegetables, or shredded meat can be added for clients who want more substance.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Bone broth has a longer history in British kitchens than almost any other dish in this book. Many clients will remember their mothers or grandmothers making stock from the Sunday roast carcass as a matter of course, and the smell of bones roasting is deeply familiar. Frame it as "proper homemade stock" rather than the more contemporary term "bone broth" for clients who might find the latter unfamiliar.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a warmed cup or small soup bowl. The dark, golden-brown colour is handsome. A single twist of lemon peel on the surface adds a fresh note. For clients who have difficulty holding a cup, a handled mug with a lid is practical and dignified.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Bone broth is naturally high in sodium from the bones themselves: season carefully and taste before adding any additional salt, particularly for clients with hypertension or heart failure. Ensure the broth is completely strained for dysphagia clients: no particles, skin, or bone fragments must remain.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: A slow cooker is the ideal vessel for bone broth: set it on low before bed and strain in the morning. The broth can be frozen in ice cube trays for very small portions and defrosted individually as needed. Butchers are often happy to give or sell bones cheaply: chicken carcasses are the easiest to source.

recipes.title: Brown Windsor Soup
recipes.about: Brown Windsor soup is one of the most quintessentially Victorian British dishes, appearing on the menus of gentlemen's clubs, railway dining cars, and country house tables throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It fell out of fashion in the mid-twentieth century and became something of a byword for institutional cooking at its worst, but a properly made Brown Windsor is a revelation: rich, deeply savoury, warming, and quite unlike the thin, tasteless version that earned it its unfortunate reputation. For clients of a certain age and background, serving it is an act of culinary archaeology.

ingredients.item: Shin of beef or braising beef, diced small

method: Season the beef pieces well with salt and pepper. Heat a heavy-based saucepan over a high heat, add a little oil, and brown the beef in batches until deeply caramelised on all sides. Do not crowd the pan. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the butter, and cook the onion, carrot, celery, and turnip for 8-10 minutes until softened.
Add the flour and tomato puree, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes. Return the beef to the pan.
Pour in the stock, add the Worcestershire sauce, thyme, and bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes until the beef is completely tender.
Remove the thyme sprigs and bay leaf. For a traditional version, blend approximately two-thirds of the soup to give a thick, rich, slightly textured result. For a fully smooth soup, blend completely.
Return to the heat, taste, and season carefully. The soup should be dark, rich, and deeply savoury.
key_nutrients: Protein and iron from the beef: excellent for muscle maintenance, wound healing, and preventing anaemia.
Collagen from the shin of beef: extracted during the long cooking, supports joint health.
Zinc from the beef: supports immune function and wound healing.
Vitamin B12: critical for neurological health, often poorly absorbed in older adults.
Carrots provide beta-carotene; turnip and celery provide fibre and vitamin C.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: one of the most powerfully nostalgic soups in this book for clients of a certain age and background. The name alone will often trigger a strong response. The rich, savoury aroma is unmistakable.
Appetite: calorie-dense from the beef and deeply savoury. The long-cooked beef flavour is often more appetising than lighter soups for clients who have lost interest in food.
Bone health: the collagen extracted from the beef shin during long cooking contributes to bone and joint support.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Blend completely until smooth and pass through a fine sieve. The beef must be completely tender before blending. Add extra warm stock if the purée is too thick.
ure the beef is completely tender. Blend or finely mince to very ll pieces under 4mm. The sauce must keep all pieces moist.
ve with a partially blended texture: rich and thick with some ll, very tender pieces of beef. Offer with soft bread for a more stantial meal.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Brown Windsor is one of the most nostalgically charged names in British culinary history. For clients who dined in clubs, hotels, or good restaurants in the mid-twentieth century it will be immediately familiar, often with a smile. It is worth telling the client you are making it by name in advance: it tends to produce a reaction. Ask whether they remember it and what they think of it.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The deep mahogany colour is the defining characteristic of this soup. Serve in a warmed white bowl. A single small piece of toasted bread or a crouton floating in the centre, and perhaps a very small sprig of thyme, is all that is needed. Do not over-garnish.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Worcestershire sauce contains gluten and anchovies: substitute with a gluten-free alternative if required. The soup is moderately high in sodium from the stock and Worcestershire sauce: taste carefully before serving and use a low-sodium stock for clients with hypertension or heart failure.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This soup benefits enormously from being made a day ahead: the flavour deepens overnight. The beef can be cooked in a slow cooker on low for 6-8 hours, then the soup finished on the stovetop. It freezes well for up to 3 months.

recipes.title: Cream of Mushroom Soup
recipes.about: A good cream of mushroom soup is one of the finest soups in the British repertoire: deeply savoury, silky, and satisfying in a way that is hard to articulate. It became a staple of British home cooking from the mid-twentieth century, when the tinned version was ubiquitous, but the homemade version is in a different category entirely. The key is to cook the mushrooms until completely concentrated and golden before adding any liquid: this step takes patience but is the difference between a good soup and an extraordinary one.

ingredients.item: Chestnut or button mushrooms, cleaned and sliced
A few drops of truffle oil (optional, for finishing)

method: Melt the butter in a large, heavy-based saucepan over a medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent.

Add the mushrooms and increase the heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 10-12 minutes until all the moisture has evaporated and the mushrooms are concentrated, golden, and beginning to caramelise at the edges. This is the most important step: do not rush it and do not add liquid until the mushrooms are completely dry.
Add the garlic and thyme, stir well, and cook for a further minute.
Sprinkle over the flour and stir to coat all the mushrooms. Cook for 2 minutes to remove the raw flour taste.
Pour in the stock gradually, stirring constantly to prevent lumps. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 10 minutes.

Remove from the heat and blend until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve for the smoothest result. Return to the pan, add the cream, and heat gently. Do not boil after adding the cream. Taste and season generously with salt and white pepper.
Serve in a warmed bowl with a swirl of cream and a few drops of truffle oil if using.
key_nutrients: Beta-glucans from the mushrooms: a form of fibre associated with immune support and cholesterol regulation.
Vitamin D: mushrooms exposed to light are one of the few plant sources of vitamin D, of particular importance for clients with limited sun exposure.
B vitamins including B2, B3, and B5: support energy metabolism and neurological function.
Selenium: an important antioxidant mineral often low in elderly diets.
Cream adds significant calories: important for clients at risk of malnutrition.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: the rich, deeply savoury aroma of concentrated mushrooms is among the most evocative of cooking smells. The familiar flavour profile of cream of mushroom soup will resonate strongly with most clients.

Appetite: the umami depth of this soup tends to stimulate appetite. The silky texture is easy to take and very satisfying. Enrich further with extra cream or a beaten egg yolk for clients who need more calories.

Dysphagia: at IDDSI Level 4 this is a naturally appropriate texture for most swallowing profiles. Ensure it is passed through a fine sieve for clients at Level 4 to remove any remaining mushroom fibres.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Blend thoroughly and pass through a fine sieve to remove any fibrous mushroom pieces. The result should be completely smooth. Check consistency: it should flow but hold its shape briefly.
Blend less thoroughly, leaving very small pieces of mushroom under 4mm. The soup must be sufficiently saucy to keep all pieces moist.
Serve smooth and creamy with a swirl of cream. Some sliced sautéed mushrooms reserved before blending and placed on top add texture and visual interest.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Cream of mushroom soup has a particular place in the British middle-class consciousness through both the tinned version, which was a staple of the 1950s-70s kitchen, and the homemade version which was a feature of dinner party starters in that era. Many clients will say immediately that it reminds them of something. The difference in quality between this and the tinned version is a worthwhile talking point.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: A uniformly dark, velvety soup benefits from careful finishing. A swirl of double cream, a few very thinly sliced raw mushrooms or small sautéed pieces on top, and a few drops of truffle oil if available make this soup look as distinguished as it tastes. Serve in a white bowl.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: This soup contains a significant amount of cream: use with caution for clients with very high cholesterol or advised to follow a low-fat diet. Reduce or substitute the cream with full-fat milk if needed. The soup thickens considerably as it cools: add extra stock when reheating.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The concentrated mushroom base can be made ahead and refrigerated for up to 2 days before adding the stock and cream. The finished soup keeps in the fridge for 2 days. It does not freeze well as the cream can split on reheating: add the cream fresh each time if freezing.

recipes.title: Cock-a-Leekie Soup
recipes.about: Cock-a-leekie is one of the oldest soups in the British Isles, with roots in Scottish cookery going back at least to the sixteenth century. It was a feature of formal Scottish dining and was well known throughout Britain by the nineteenth century. The traditional recipe includes prunes, which add a gentle sweetness and depth that balances the savoury chicken and leek perfectly. For clients of a certain background and age, this is a dish of considerable historical and personal resonance: refined, comforting, and deeply nourishing.

ingredients.item: Chicken thighs on the bone, skin removed
Leeks, washed and sliced into rounds
Prunes, stoned and halved (traditional: do not omit)

method: Place the chicken thighs in a large saucepan. Pour over the stock, add the thyme, bay leaf, and pearl barley if using. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer. Skim off any foam that rises.
Add half the sliced leeks to the simmering pot. Cook gently for 1 hour until the chicken is completely tender and falling from the bone.
Remove the chicken thighs and set aside to cool slightly. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs and bay leaf.
Add the remaining fresh leeks and the prunes to the simmering broth. Cook for a further 15-20 minutes until the leeks are completely soft and the prunes have partially dissolved into the broth.
Meanwhile, pick the chicken meat from the bones, discarding all skin and bone. Shred the meat into small, tender pieces.
Return the shredded chicken to the soup. Taste and season carefully. Stir in the chopped parsley.
Serve in a warmed bowl: a golden, fragrant broth with soft leeks, tender chicken, and the sweet note of the prunes.
key_nutrients: Lean protein from the chicken thighs: excellent for muscle maintenance and wound healing.
Fibre from the prunes: one of the most effective dietary interventions for constipation, which is endemic in elderly care.
Potassium from the leeks: supports heart health and blood pressure.
Sorbitol in prunes: a natural laxative effect that supports bowel regularity.
Pearl barley adds fibre and a low-GI carbohydrate source, supporting sustained energy release.
good_for_conditions: Appetite: the combination of chicken, leeks, and sweet prunes is unusual enough to be interesting without being unfamiliar. The golden broth is deeply appetising.
Dementia: a dish of considerable historical resonance for clients of British and particularly Scottish heritage. Mentioning the name is often enough to trigger a response.
Heart health: very low in saturated fat. The chicken, leeks, and barley are all associated with cardiovascular benefit.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Blend the entire soup until completely smooth, including the prunes which blend to a smooth, sweet enrichment. Pass through a fine sieve. The result is a rich, golden, sweet-savoury purée.
Finely shred the chicken into very small pieces under 4mm. Chop the leeks finely. The prunes will be very soft: chop finely. Ensure plenty of broth to keep everything moist.
Serve as made: a clear, golden broth with tender shreds of chicken, soft leeks, and plump prunes. A classic and beautiful soup.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Cock-a-leekie has a particularly strong resonance for clients of Scottish heritage but is widely known across Britain. The inclusion of prunes often surprises clients who do not remember this detail: it is always worth mentioning and tends to prompt a discussion about whether they have encountered the traditional version before. Many clients will not have tasted it in decades.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve as a clear broth with visible pieces of tender chicken, soft leeks, and soft, dark prunes. It is a handsome soup that needs no garnish beyond a little flat-leaf parsley. Serve in a warmed wide bowl so the broth and its contents can be seen clearly.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: The prunes have a laxative effect and should be used with some awareness if the client already has digestive sensitivity. Reduce to 3 prunes for clients who are prone to loose stools. Pearl barley contains gluten: omit for clients with coeliac disease or gluten intolerance.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This soup is ideally made in a slow cooker: place all ingredients together and cook on low for 6-8 hours. The chicken will be falling from the bone. It keeps in the fridge for 3 days and freezes very well for up to 3 months.

recipes.title: Spiced Carrot and Coriander Soup
recipes.about: Carrot and coriander soup became one of the most popular homemade soups in Britain during the 1980s and 1990s and is likely to be one of the most familiar dishes in this chapter for clients in their 70s and 80s. It is bright, warming, naturally sweet, and beautifully coloured. The coriander adds a gentle aromatic quality that lifts the sweetness of the carrots without overpowering them. It is among the simplest soups to make well, and it rarely fails to please.

ingredients.item: Fresh coriander leaves and stalks, roughly chopped

method: Heat the butter or oil in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook for 6-8 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the garlic, ground coriander, and cumin. Stir and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the diced carrots and stir to coat in the spiced onion mixture.
Pour in the stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20-25 minutes until the carrots are completely tender when pierced with a knife.
Add the fresh coriander, stalks and all. Remove from the heat and blend until completely smooth.
Return to the heat, stir in the cream if using, and heat through gently. Taste and season with salt and white pepper.
Serve in a warmed bowl with a swirl of cream and a few small fresh coriander leaves if the client enjoys them.
key_nutrients: Beta-carotene from the carrots: converted to vitamin A in the body, important for immune function, vision, and skin health. One of the richest vegetable sources available.
Anti-inflammatory compounds from the coriander and cumin: support digestive health and reduce systemic inflammation.
Vitamin K from the carrots and fresh coriander: supports bone health and blood clotting.
Fibre: supports digestive regularity and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.
Naturally low in fat and calories before cream is added: suitable for clients monitoring calorie intake.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: carrots, coriander, and cumin are all associated with cardiovascular benefit. A naturally low-fat soup before cream is added. Use olive oil rather than butter for clients with elevated cholesterol.
Diabetes: carrots have a low glycaemic load in soup form. The fibre content slows sugar absorption. A good choice for clients managing blood sugar, particularly served without bread.
Cancer support: the beta-carotene content of carrots is among the highest of any vegetable. Anti-inflammatory spices contribute additional protective compounds.

iddsi_table.adaptation: The carrots blend to a very smooth consistency. Pass through a fine sieve for the smoothest result. Adjust consistency with extra warm stock as needed.
Blend less thoroughly, ensuring all pieces are under 4mm. The soup should be well sauced to keep the pieces moist.
Serve smooth and vivid orange. A swirl of cream and a few coriander leaves finish it well. Offer a small piece of warm crusty bread alongside for clients who can manage it.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Carrot and coriander soup became fashionable in the 1980s alongside the broader interest in fresh, homemade cooking that characterised that era. Many clients will have made it themselves or encountered it in restaurants and dinner parties. It has the particular quality of feeling both familiar and slightly special, which makes it an ideal choice for a simple lunch that nonetheless feels considered.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The vivid orange colour of this soup is its greatest visual asset. Serve in a white bowl to contrast. A swirl of cream, a few fresh coriander leaves (for clients who enjoy them), and a few drops of olive oil make a clean, attractive finish. The soup should be smooth and glossy.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Some clients dislike fresh coriander intensely: always check before serving. Ground coriander (the spice) is milder and less divisive than the fresh herb, so the soup can be made without the fresh herb if preferred. Carrots are relatively low in potassium compared to other vegetables and are generally safe for clients with mild CKD, but check the care plan.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: This is one of the quickest soups in the chapter to make from start to finish. It keeps in the fridge for 3 days and freezes for up to 3 months. The flavour improves overnight. Reheat gently, adding a splash of stock to restore the smooth consistency.

recipes.title: Potted Shrimps with Brown Bread
recipes.about: Potted shrimps are one of the great British seaside delicacies, with roots in the eighteenth century and a strong association with Morecambe Bay. Tiny brown shrimps set in spiced clarified butter, served with brown bread: a dish of absolute simplicity and considerable refinement. For clients who ate well throughout their lives, this is a starter of real pleasure. It requires almost no cooking and can be prepared quickly on any day.

ingredients.item: Brown bread, thinly sliced and buttered

method: Melt the butter in a small saucepan over a gentle heat. Add the mace, cayenne, and nutmeg. Stir gently.
Add the shrimps and warm through for 1-2 minutes only. Do not overheat. Add a few drops of lemon juice and taste.
Spoon into a small ramekin, pressing the shrimps down gently. Pour the spiced butter over to just cover. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes until set.
Remove from the fridge 10 minutes before serving. Serve with thin brown bread and butter and a wedge of lemon.
key_nutrients: Protein from the shrimps: a lean, complete protein source supporting muscle maintenance.
Iodine: shrimps are one of the richest dietary sources, important for thyroid function.
Vitamin B12: supports neurological function.
Butter provides fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and significant calories.
Low carbohydrate: suitable for clients managing blood sugar.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: potted shrimps are associated strongly with seaside holidays and formal dining. The name and presentation both tend to provoke a warm response.
Appetite: rich and buttery, served in a small portion. Ideal before a main course for clients with limited appetite.
Heart health: shrimps are low in saturated fat. Use a slightly lighter hand with the butter for clients with cardiovascular concerns.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made with brown bread.
Shrimps are already very small. Serve on soft bread without crusts.
Finely chop the shrimps and mix with the spiced butter. Serve on very soft moistened bread.
Blend the shrimps and spiced butter until completely smooth. Pass through a sieve. Serve as a smooth pate.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Potted shrimps are associated with a certain style of British dining: seaside hotels, gentlemen's clubs, the kind of lunch once taken seriously. Many clients will not have encountered them in years. Placing a small ramekin on the table is itself an event.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve the ramekin on a small plate with a wedge of lemon and two thin slices of brown bread and butter, crusts removed and cut into triangles.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Check for shellfish allergy. Cayenne and mace are very mild here but omit for clients with sensitive digestion. Ensure the butter has come to room temperature before serving or it will be too firm.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days once set. Make in the morning and serve at lunch with no further work.

recipes.title: Avocado and Prawn Cocktail
condition_tags: ! High in potassium from the avocado: avoid or reduce for clients with chronic kidney
recipes.about: Prawn cocktail was the defining British dinner party starter from the 1960s through the 1980s, appearing on virtually every celebration table. With avocado, fashionable since the 1970s, it becomes more substantial and nutritionally valuable. For clients of this generation it carries very strong nostalgic associations with occasions and celebrations.
method: Make the Marie Rose sauce: mix the mayonnaise, ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, and lemon juice. Taste and adjust.
Shred the lettuce and arrange in a small glass or bowl.
Fan or dice the avocado and arrange alongside the lettuce.
Toss the prawns in half the Marie Rose sauce and spoon over. Drizzle the remaining sauce over.
Dust with paprika. Serve with thin brown bread and butter.
key_nutrients: Monounsaturated fats from the avocado: strongly associated with heart health.
Potassium from the avocado: supports blood pressure regulation.
Protein from the prawns: lean and complete.
Vitamin E from the avocado: a powerful antioxidant.
Folate: important for cell repair.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: avocado and prawns both associated with cardiovascular benefit.
Diabetes: a low-carbohydrate starter. The avocado provides healthy fats that slow glucose absorption.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Prawns are tender and avocado naturally soft.
Cut prawns and avocado into small pieces under 1.5cm.
Finely chop prawns and mash avocado. Combine with sauce to a moist mixture.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Few dishes carry as much nostalgic weight for this generation as prawn cocktail. Many clients will associate it immediately with Christmas dinner or a special restaurant. The glass presentation is important: it signals occasion.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a stemmed glass if possible. Prawns visible on top, paprika dusting, lemon on the rim.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Check for shellfish allergy. Worcestershire sauce contains gluten and anchovies. Avocado must be ripe: check the day before.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Marie Rose sauce keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Do not slice the avocado until just before serving.

recipes.title: Chicken Liver Pate on Toast
recipes.about: Chicken liver pate is one of the most underrated dishes in British cookery: quick, extraordinarily nutritious, and of a richness that belies its simplicity. It was a staple of the British dinner party from the 1960s onwards. The keys are not overcooking the livers and using enough butter.

ingredients.item: Toast or soft bread to serve

method: Melt half the butter in a frying pan. Cook the shallot for 3-4 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and thyme.
Increase the heat. Add the livers and cook 2-3 minutes each side. They should be browned outside but slightly pink within. Do not overcook.
Add the brandy if using and allow to bubble for 30 seconds.
Transfer to a blender with the cream and remaining butter. Blend until smooth. Season well.
Pass through a sieve, spoon into a ramekin, refrigerate for at least 1 hour. Serve with toast and cornichons.
key_nutrients: Iron: one of the single richest dietary sources available, far exceeding red meat.
Vitamin A: liver is the most concentrated food source.
Vitamin B12: extremely rich. One serving provides several times the daily requirement.
Folate: important for cell repair and reducing cognitive decline risk.
Zinc: supports immune function and wound healing.
good_for_conditions: Appetite: richness and depth of flavour very effective at stimulating appetite. A small amount is nutritionally significant.
Dementia: familiar from dinner parties and entertaining. The smell of the livers cooking is itself a positive trigger.
Cancer support: extraordinary nutrient density makes liver one of the most valuable foods in cancer care.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve spread on hot toast. Offer cornichons alongside.
Serve a generous spoonful on soft bread without crusts, cut small.
The pate is already smooth if passed through a sieve. Thin with a little cream to achieve correct IDDSI 4 consistency.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Chicken liver pate is associated with the careful home entertaining of the 1960s-70s, often from a Robert Carrier or Elizabeth David recipe. Ask if the client has a recipe they used to use.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a small ramekin, hot toast cut into soldiers, two or three cornichons alongside.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Very high in vitamin A: check for clients on high-dose supplements. Do not serve to clients who dislike offal without asking first.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Keeps in the fridge for 4 days sealed with butter. Freezes for 1 month.

recipes.title: Soft Boiled Egg with Soldiers
recipes.about: A perfectly soft-boiled egg with buttered soldiers is one of the most elemental pleasures of British breakfast and lunch culture. For many elderly clients it is deeply associated with childhood: a Sunday morning, a sick day in bed, a grandmother's kitchen. It requires almost no skill but considerable attention to timing.

ingredients.item: Large free-range egg, at room temperature

method: Bring a small saucepan of water to a rolling boil. Gently lower the egg in. Set a timer for exactly 6 minutes for a runny yolk, or 7 minutes for a slightly firmer yolk.
While the egg cooks, toast the bread and butter it generously while hot. Cut into soldiers approximately 2cm wide.
When the timer sounds, remove the egg and place in an egg cup. Cut the top off.
Season the yolk lightly. Serve immediately with the soldiers.
key_nutrients: Complete protein: eggs contain all essential amino acids in near-perfect proportions.
Vitamin D: one of the few reliable food sources. Important for bone health.
Choline: essential for brain health. Eggs are the richest dietary source.
Lutein and zeaxanthin: support eye health.
B vitamins including B2, B12, and folate.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: few dishes carry more nostalgic weight. Associated universally with being looked after. The tactile pleasure of dipping the soldier is valuable.
Appetite: small, complete, and manageable. An excellent choice for clients not hungry enough for a full meal.
Bone health: vitamin D and protein both contribute to bone density maintenance.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made.
Scoop the egg from the shell and serve in a small bowl. Cut bread small.
Scramble the egg softly. Serve on very soft well-buttered bread without crusts.
Blend a softly scrambled egg with butter and a little cream until smooth.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: There is almost no client for whom a boiled egg and soldiers will not produce an immediate warm response. Ask how they like their egg: 6 minutes or 7. That small act of asking gives them control and signals attentiveness.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Use a proper egg cup. Soldiers cut neatly alongside. A small pinch of paprika on the yolk is a nice touch.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Timing is everything. Use a timer without exception. Ensure the egg white is fully set for clients with compromised immune systems.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Once you know the client's preference, entirely reliable. A phone timer every time removes all uncertainty.

recipes.title: Smooth Mackerel Pate with Cucumber
recipes.about: Smoked mackerel pate is one of the most effortless things a carer can make, requiring no cooking whatsoever. Smoked mackerel has a deep savoury intensity that cream cheese smooths into something spreadable and elegant. It became fashionable in British home cooking in the 1970s and 80s and will be immediately familiar to most clients.

ingredients.item: Smoked mackerel fillets, skinned and flaked

method: Check the mackerel carefully for bones. Place in a food processor with the cream cheese, horseradish, and lemon juice.
Blend until smooth but with a little texture remaining. Taste and adjust lemon and pepper.
For a completely smooth result, pass through a sieve.
Spoon into a small dish. Refrigerate for 20 minutes. Serve with cucumber, toast or oatcakes, and dill.
key_nutrients: Omega-3 fatty acids: mackerel is among the richest fish sources, strongly associated with brain and heart health.
Protein from both the mackerel and cream cheese.
Vitamin D: oily fish is one of the best dietary sources.
Calcium from the cream cheese.
Iodine from the fish: supports thyroid function.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: omega-3 rich oily fish is one of the most evidence-based dietary interventions for cardiovascular health.
Dementia: omega-3 DHA is strongly associated with brain health and reduced dementia risk.
Bone health: vitamin D from the mackerel and calcium from the cream cheese support bone density.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made with toast or oatcakes and cucumber.
Serve on soft bread without crusts, cut small. Slice cucumber very thinly or omit.
Blend completely smooth and pass through a fine sieve. Thin with a little cream if needed.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Smoked mackerel pate became a fixture of the British kitchen in the 1970s when smoked fish became more available. Many clients will have made it themselves or encountered it at dinner parties.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a small ramekin with cucumber alongside, a few sprigs of dill, and oatcakes or toast triangles.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Check for fish allergy. Horseradish can cause gastric irritation: reduce or omit for clients with reflux. Ensure all bones are removed before blending.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: No cooking required. Takes under 10 minutes. Keeps in the fridge for 3 days.

recipes.title: Angels on Horseback
condition_tags: ! High in sodium from the bacon. Contains molluscs: check for shellfish allergy.
recipes.about: Angels on horseback are among the most quintessentially British of all savouries: oysters wrapped in bacon and grilled, served on toast. They appeared on Victorian and Edwardian dinner tables as a savoury course after pudding. For clients of a certain background, they carry an almost ceremonial quality and tend to provoke both surprise and pleasure.

ingredients.item: Fresh oysters, shucked, or tinned smoked oysters

method: Pat the oysters dry. Season with black pepper.
Wrap each oyster in a rasher of streaky bacon. Secure with a cocktail stick if needed.
Place on a baking tray under a very hot grill. Cook for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until the bacon is golden.
Butter the toast and cut into small squares. Remove the cocktail sticks.
Arrange on the toast. Serve immediately, very hot.
key_nutrients: Zinc from the oysters: one of the richest dietary sources. Critical for immune function.
Vitamin B12: oysters are extraordinarily rich, supporting neurological health.
Iron and selenium: important for energy and immune function.
Protein from both the oysters and bacon.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: a dish of strong cultural resonance for clients from backgrounds where formal dining was part of life.
Appetite: savoury, rich, and served in small individual pieces. The contrast of crisp bacon and soft oyster is stimulating.
Heart health: the oysters are excellent for heart health. Use leaner back bacon for clients with cardiovascular concerns.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Both oyster and well-cooked bacon should be tender enough for most clients.
Ensure bacon is very well cooked until completely soft. Cut into small pieces under 1.5cm.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Angels on horseback represent a world of British dining that has largely vanished: the savoury course, served after the pudding on a starched tablecloth. Many clients from certain backgrounds will have a vivid fond memory of them.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve neatly arranged on buttered toast. Must be served immediately.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Both dishes are high in sodium from the bacon. Limit frequency for clients with hypertension or heart failure. The bacon must be cooked until fully tender, not crispy. Crispy or chewy bacon is a choking risk for clients with any dental difficulty or reduced chewing ability. These dishes are suitable at IDDSI Level 7 only and should not be offered to clients below this level. Serve immediately from the grill.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Can be prepared (wrapped) up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Grill just before serving. Tinned smoked oysters work very well.

recipes.title: Devils on Horseback
recipes.about: Devils on horseback are the prune-filled cousin of angels on horseback: the sweetness of the prune against the salty, smoky bacon is a combination of real sophistication. Like angels on horseback, they were served as a Victorian savoury course. The prunes also provide one of the most effective dietary interventions for constipation in elderly clients.
method: Wrap each prune tightly in a rasher of streaky bacon. Secure with a cocktail stick if needed.
Place on a baking tray under a very hot grill. Cook for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until the bacon is golden.
Butter the toast and cut into small squares. Remove the cocktail sticks.
Arrange on the toast. Serve immediately.
key_nutrients: Fibre from the prunes: highly effective for relieving constipation. Prunes contain sorbitol, a natural laxative, and high levels of soluble fibre.
Potassium from the prunes: supports heart health.
Vitamin K: important for bone health.
Iron from the prunes.
Protein from the bacon.
good_for_conditions: Appetite: the sweet-savoury combination is unusual and stimulating to the palate.
Dementia: the name alone tends to produce a reaction of delight.
Bone health: vitamin K from the prunes contributes to bone density maintenance.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Prunes are naturally soft.
Ensure bacon is very well cooked and soft. Cut into small pieces under 1.5cm.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Devils on horseback carry the same ceremonial quality as angels on horseback. The sweet prune and salty bacon combination surprises and delights most clients.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Arranged neatly on buttered toast, served immediately and very hot. A pinch of cayenne is the traditional finish.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Both dishes are high in sodium from the bacon. Limit frequency for clients with hypertension or heart failure. The bacon must be cooked until fully tender, not crispy. Crispy or chewy bacon is a choking risk for clients with any dental difficulty or reduced chewing ability. These dishes are suitable at IDDSI Level 7 only and should not be offered to clients below this level. High in sodium from the bacon: limit for clients with hypertension.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Can be prepared ahead and grilled to order.

recipes.title: Potted Beef with Toast
recipes.about: Potted beef is one of the oldest British preserves: slow-cooked beef pounded with butter and spices, sealed with clarified butter and served cold. It appears in British cookery books from the seventeenth century onwards. The result is something between a pate and a spreadable beef paste: intensely savoury and richly buttered. It is rarely seen today, which makes it all the more worth making.

ingredients.item: Braising or shin of beef, diced
Toast or crusty bread to serve

method: Place the beef in a small ovenproof dish with a tight-fitting lid. Add 20g butter, the spices, Worcestershire sauce, and seasoning. Add just enough water to barely cover.
Cover and cook at 150°C / 130°C fan for 2-2.5 hours until the beef is completely tender.
Drain the beef, reserving the cooking liquid. Cool slightly.
Shred the beef finely, then beat or pulse in a processor until fibres break down. Do not over-process.
Beat in remaining softened butter. Add a little cooking liquid. Season generously.
Pack into small ramekins. Seal with clarified butter. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Serve with hot toast.
key_nutrients: Protein from the beef: excellent for muscle maintenance and wound healing.
Iron and zinc: beef is one of the richest sources of both.
Vitamin B12: critical for neurological health.
Collagen from the slow cooking: supports joint health.
Significant calories from the butter.
good_for_conditions: Appetite: intensely flavoured and rich. A small amount is nutritionally significant.
Dementia: potted beef is associated with a now-rare tradition of British larder cooking.
Bone health: collagen from the long cooking contributes to joint and bone support.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve slightly softened on hot toast.
Serve a generous spoonful on soft bread without crusts.
Process more thoroughly until completely smooth. Add extra butter and a little warm cooking liquid. Pass through a sieve.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Potted beef represents a world of British domestic cooking that has almost entirely disappeared: the larder, the preserving tradition, the careful use of every cut. Many clients from rural backgrounds will have strong memories of potted meats.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in the ramekin with a clarified butter seal on top. Hot toast alongside. Simple and considered.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Worcestershire sauce contains gluten and anchovies. Allow to come fully to room temperature before serving or it will be very firm.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: Makes a large batch: keeps in the fridge for 5 days, sealed with butter. Freezes for 2 months.

recipes.title: Smoked Salmon with Brown Bread and Butter
recipes.about: Smoked salmon with brown bread and butter is a British classic of the highest order: effortless, elegant, and deeply pleasurable. It has been a staple of the British celebration table since the nineteenth century and remains associated with occasions and special treatment. For clients who ate well, this is a dish that signals consideration and respect. It requires no cooking, only good ingredients.

ingredients.item: Fresh dill or watercress to serve

method: Remove the smoked salmon from the fridge 5 minutes before serving.
Butter the brown bread generously. Remove crusts if preferred. Cut into small triangles.
Drape the salmon loosely over one side of the plate. It should look relaxed, not flat.
Arrange the bread alongside. Add lemon, black pepper, and capers or dill.
Serve immediately.
key_nutrients: Omega-3 fatty acids: smoked salmon is one of the richest sources, supporting brain and heart health.
Protein: complete and easily absorbed.
Vitamin D: one of the best dietary sources.
Vitamin B12: critical for neurological function.
Calcium from the bread.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: omega-3 fatty acids from salmon are strongly cardioprotective.
Dementia: omega-3 DHA from oily fish is consistently associated with reduced cognitive decline.
Bone health: vitamin D from the salmon and calcium from the bread both contribute.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Smoked salmon is naturally soft and tender.
Cut into very small pieces under 1.5cm. Serve on soft bread without crusts.
Finely chop the salmon and mix with softened butter and lemon juice to a moist mixture.
Blend with cream cheese and lemon juice until completely smooth. Thin with a little cream if needed.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Smoked salmon has been a marker of occasion and generosity in British life for generations. Serving it on a weekday, unexpectedly, as a small act of generosity, is particularly effective at lifting a client's day.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: White plate. Salmon draped loosely, bread triangles neatly arranged, lemon wedge, a small amount of greenery. Simplicity.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Very high in sodium: limit for clients with hypertension, heart failure, or CKD. Buy the best quality available.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: No cooking required. 5 minutes preparation. An ideal option when time is very short.

recipes.title: Pan-Fried Salmon with Lemon Butter
recipes.about: A perfectly pan-fried salmon fillet with a simple lemon butter sauce is one of the finest quick fish dishes in British cooking. The key is a very hot pan, dry fish, and the confidence to leave it alone while it cooks. The skin should be golden and crisp, the flesh just cooked through with the faintest trace of pink at the centre. The lemon butter takes seconds and transforms the dish.
method: Remove the salmon from the fridge 10 minutes before cooking. Pat completely dry with kitchen paper.
Season the flesh side generously. Heat a pan over a high heat until very hot. Add the olive oil.
Place the salmon skin-side down. Press gently for 30 seconds. Do not move it. Cook for 5-6 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and the flesh has turned opaque two-thirds of the way up.
Flip carefully. Cook for 1-2 further minutes. Remove and rest on a warm plate.
Reduce heat. Add the butter to the same pan, allow to foam and turn golden. Add the lemon juice, swirl, and add the parsley.
Pour the lemon butter over the resting salmon. Serve immediately.
key_nutrients: Omega-3 fatty acids: salmon is one of the richest sources. DHA and EPA support brain, heart, and reduce inflammation.
Vitamin D: salmon provides more per serving than almost any other food.
Protein: complete and highly bioavailable.
Vitamin B12 and B6: important for neurological function.
Selenium: an important antioxidant mineral.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: one of the most evidence-based dietary choices for cardiovascular health.
Dementia: regular oily fish consistently associated with reduced cognitive decline.
Bone health: vitamin D content supports calcium absorption and bone density.
Diabetes: very low carbohydrate with minimal blood sugar impact.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made with crisp skin. Ensure all pin bones removed.
Remove the skin. Flake into small pieces under 1.5cm. Moisten with lemon butter.
Flake finely and mix with lemon butter until cohesive and moist. All pieces under 4mm.
Blend with lemon butter and a little cream until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Pan-fried salmon became fashionable in Britain from the 1980s as fresh salmon became widely available. Many clients will have eaten it regularly in good restaurants or cooked it themselves.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve skin-side up so the golden skin remains crisp. Lemon butter poured over. A lemon wedge on the side, a few new potatoes, and some wilted spinach.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Check carefully for pin bones before cooking. The lemon butter spatters when juice hits the hot butter: stand back slightly.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The lemon butter can be made ahead and kept in the fridge. Reheat gently before serving.

recipes.title: Baked Cod with Parsley Sauce
recipes.about: Baked cod with parsley sauce is one of the most traditional and enduring British fish dishes, appearing in cookery books from the Victorian era and remaining on family tables throughout the twentieth century. It is gentle, nutritious, and deeply familiar. The parsley sauce, a simple bechamel with fresh parsley, is one of the classic British sauces and transforms a piece of white fish into something complete and satisfying.
method: Preheat the oven to 180°C / 160°C fan / Gas 4.
Place the cod in a small ovenproof dish. Dot with butter, season lightly. Cover with foil.
Bake for 15-18 minutes until just opaque throughout and flaking easily. Do not overcook.

Make the sauce: melt the butter, add the flour, cook for 2 minutes stirring. Add the milk gradually, stirring constantly. Bring to a simmer until the sauce thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 5-6 minutes.
Remove from heat. Stir in the parsley and season with salt, white pepper, and nutmeg.
Serve the cod with the parsley sauce poured over.
key_nutrients: Protein from the cod: very lean, complete protein. Excellent for clients who need protein without additional fat.
Iodine: white fish is one of the richest dietary sources, important for thyroid function.
Calcium from the milk in the sauce.
B vitamins including B6 and B12.
Phosphorus: supports bone health.
good_for_conditions: Heart health: cod is very low in saturated fat. A genuinely heart-friendly dish.
Kidney friendly: white fish like cod is lower in potassium and phosphorus than oily fish. Always check the care plan for specific restrictions.
Diabetes: high protein, very low carbohydrate from the fish.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made with parsley sauce poured over.
Cod is naturally flaky. Ensure all pieces under 1.5cm and well-moistened with the sauce.
Flake the cod very finely and mix thoroughly with the parsley sauce until cohesive throughout.
Blend the flaked cod with the parsley sauce and extra milk until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Baked cod with parsley sauce is one of the most universally recognised British fish dishes of the twentieth century. Associated strongly with school dinners, hospital meals, and home cooking of a certain era. Comforting precisely because it is so familiar.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: The parsley sauce should be vivid green-flecked white. Pour generously. Boiled new potatoes and buttered peas alongside.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Cod overcooks quickly. Check at 15 minutes. Check carefully for pin bones. The parsley sauce must be well-seasoned.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The parsley sauce can be made ahead and reheated gently with a splash of extra milk. Good-quality frozen cod works perfectly.

recipes.title: Fish Pie
recipes.about: Fish pie is one of the great British comfort dishes: creamy, warming, and deeply satisfying, with a golden mashed potato crust concealing a filling of tender fish in a rich sauce. It appears in British cookery books from the Victorian era and has remained a household staple ever since. It is also one of the most adaptable dishes in this book.
method: Preheat the oven to 190°C / 170°C fan / Gas 5.
Place the fish in a saucepan with the milk and bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 5 minutes. Remove the fish and reserve the milk. Discard the bay leaf.
Make the sauce: melt the butter, add the flour, cook for 2 minutes. Add the reserved milk gradually until a smooth sauce forms. Simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in the cream and parsley. Season well.
Flake the cooked fish into large pieces, checking carefully for bones. Add to the sauce with the prawns if using. Pour into an ovenproof dish.
Cook the potatoes until tender. Drain and mash with butter and milk until smooth. Season well.
Spoon the mash over the fish filling, spreading evenly and creating a ridged surface with a fork.
Bake for 25-30 minutes until golden and bubbling. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.
key_nutrients: Protein from multiple fish sources: white fish and smoked fish together provide excellent complete protein.
Calcium and vitamin D from the milk and fish.
Iodine: white fish and smoked fish are excellent sources.
Significant calories from the cream, butter, and mash: excellent for clients needing enrichment.
good_for_conditions: Bone health: milk, cream, and fish all contribute calcium and vitamin D.
Heart health: use less cream and butter for clients with cardiovascular concerns.
Appetite: one of the most comforting and well-received dishes in elderly care.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Ensure all fish bones removed before baking.
Ensure all fish flaked to small pieces under 1.5cm. The mash and sauce keep everything moist.
Blend or finely chop all fish to very small pieces under 4mm. Mix with extra sauce.
Blend the filling with extra sauce until completely smooth. Blend the mash separately. Pass each through a sieve.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Fish pie is a dish of almost universal nostalgic warmth in Britain. Associated with family Sunday lunches and school term-time suppers. Many clients will say it is one of their favourite dishes.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in the dish it was baked in. The golden mash surface should arrive intact.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Check very carefully for pin bones before adding fish to the sauce. Smoked haddock is high in sodium: use sparingly for hypertensive clients.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The filling can be made a day ahead and kept in the fridge. Top with mash and bake when needed. Freezes well in individual portions.

recipes.title: Kedgeree
recipes.about: Kedgeree is the great Anglo-Indian breakfast dish: flaked smoked haddock, basmati rice, soft-boiled eggs, butter, and a gentle warmth of curry spice. It appears in British cookery books from the mid-nineteenth century and was a fixture of the Victorian breakfast sideboard. It is one of the most distinctively British dishes in existence.
method: Poach the smoked haddock in the milk with a bay leaf for 8-10 minutes. Remove, reserving the milk. Flake carefully, removing all skin and bones.
Cook the rice in salted water until just tender. Drain.
Melt the butter in a large pan. Cook the onion gently for 6-8 minutes. Add the curry powder and turmeric, cook for 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice and stir to coat. Add a few tablespoons of the reserved poaching milk to loosen.
Fold in the flaked haddock gently. Taste and season carefully.
Serve topped with the soft-boiled egg halves, parsley, and a wedge of lemon.
key_nutrients: Protein from both the fish and the eggs: complete and highly bioavailable.
Iodine from the smoked haddock: one of the richest dietary sources.
Turmeric: contains curcumin, a powerful anti-inflammatory compound.
B vitamins from the eggs and fish.
Carbohydrate from the rice: sustained energy release.
good_for_conditions: Dementia: kedgeree is one of the most culturally distinctive British dishes, carrying very strong associations for clients of certain backgrounds.
Appetite: the combination of warm spice, creamy fish, and soft egg is deeply comforting.
Diabetes: basmati rice has a lower glycaemic index than other varieties.

iddsi_table.adaptation: Serve as made. Ensure all skin and bones removed.
Flake the haddock very finely. Ensure rice is very soft. Cut egg into very small pieces. Moisten with extra poaching milk.

carer_tips.nostalgia_note: Kedgeree occupies a unique place in British culinary history. For clients from certain backgrounds it is strongly associated with weekend breakfasts and country house visits. The smell of the curry spice warming in the butter is itself evocative.
carer_tips.presentation_tip: Serve in a wide, shallow bowl. Yellow turmeric-stained rice, white flakes of fish, golden egg halves. A wedge of lemon and a scattering of green herb.
carer_tips.watch_out_for: Smoked haddock is high in sodium: use undyed where possible. Check very carefully for bones.
carer_tips.make_it_easier: The rice can be cooked ahead. The whole dish comes together in under 30 minutes.

recipes.title: Sardines on Toast
recipes.about: Sardines on toast is one of the simplest and most nutritionally valuable dishes a carer can make. Tinned sardines are extraordinarily rich in omega-3 fatty acids, calcium from the edible bones, vitamin D, and protein. A single tin packs more nutritional value than many far more complicated dishes. Many clients will have eaten them regularly throughout their lives.

ingredients.item: Tinned sardines in olive oil, drained
Flat-leaf parsley or watercress to serve

method: Toast the bread and butter it while still hot.
Drain the sardines and lay them on the toast. Press gently with a fork.
Add a squeeze of lemon juice, a dash of Worcestershire sauce, and a grind of black pepper.
Serve immediately with parsley or watercress alongside.
key_nutrients: Omega-3 fatty acids: tinned sardines are among the very richest dietary sources of EPA and DHA.
Calcium: the soft, edible bones provide more calcium per serving than a glass of milk.
Vitamin D: one of the best dietary sources available.
Protein: complete and very easily absorbed.
Vitamin B12: extremely high content.
